verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ... אֲרוֹנוֹ בָּא
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates the actual death of Ulla and the physical transport of his coffin, which are physical events in the world.

stories.summary: A man asks Rabbi Hanina if he should travel to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage for his deceased brother's widow, and is harshly rebuked.

verdict_obj.why: The passage describes a man approaching a sage to ask a legal question about a hypothetical journey, which is a standard framing for a legal query rather than a narrated event.

stories.summary: Rabba's brothers send him a letter from Eretz Yisrael urging him to immigrate, citing an anecdote about a man who died for leaving the land and offering health advice.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: was suffering through his love... suffered without leaving the country until the day he died
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: מִצְטַעֵר עַל אִשָּׁה אַחַת... גִּלְגֵּל בְּעַצְמוֹ עַד יוֹם מוֹתוֹ
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific incident (Ma'aseh) involving a man's emotional suffering and his physical endurance/death in the land of Israel.

stories.summary: An incident is recorded where a turnip grew so large that a fox nested inside it.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: a fox that nested inside a turnip, and they weighed this turnip, and they discovered
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific past incident involving physical actions: a fox nesting in a turnip and people weighing and measuring the object.

stories.summary: An Amorite asks a resident of Israel about the yield of a palm tree and mocks him for 'destroying' the land's bounty with such high yields.

verdict_obj.why: The entire passage consists of a verbal exchange between two individuals regarding the yield of a tree, with no physical actions or emotional changes narrated as actually occurring.

stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar marks three milestones in his career in Israel, noting how each one fulfills a condition to escape a biblical curse.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: ascended to Eretz Yisrael
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates the physical travel of Rabbi Elazar from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, which is a physical event.

stories.summary: Rav Kahana accepted a scarf as payment for the redemption of a firstborn son, declaring that to him personally, it was worth the required five sela.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: took a cloth
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a physical action where Rav Kahana takes an object (a cloth) as part of a redemption ceremony.

stories.summary: Mar bar Rav Ashi purchased a scarf from the mother of Rabbah of Paraziya to demonstrate its value.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: Mar bar Rav Ashi bought a cloth
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי זְבַן סוּדָרָא
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific historical transaction where Mar bar Rav Ashi physically purchased a head-covering.

stories.summary: A man betroths a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya physically examines the item to see if it meets the minimum value for a valid betrothal.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: examined the bundle
verdict_obj.why: The passage describes a physical action where Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya actively examines a physical object (a bundle of rags) to determine its material value.

stories.summary: Following Rav Hisda's ruling that a betrothal with a marble was invalid, the woman remarried and had children, but the Sages of Sura avoided marrying into her family due to the halakhic dispute.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: the Sages avoided the family and refused to marry into it
verdict_obj.why: The passage describes a physical social boycott and the act of avoiding/separating from a specific family, which constitutes a physical event in the world beyond mere legal deliberation.

stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in a marketplace, and Rav Yosef ruled that he should be flogged for the impropriety and provide a bill of divorce.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific physical act of betrothal using an object in a public space as a historical event that triggered the subsequent legal query.

stories.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house immersed in a mikveh, but a bone was later found between her teeth, raising questions about the validity of the immersion.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: immersed herself, and she ascended from her immersion and a bone was found
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific historical incident involving physical actions: a maidservant immersing in a ritual bath, exiting the bath, and the discovery of a physical object (a bone) in her mouth.

stories.summary: While traveling on a ship, Rabban Gamliel designates tithes and rents the land they sit on to other sages to effect the transfer.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: were traveling on a ship
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a physical journey (traveling on a ship) as a historical event rather than a hypothetical case or a static scene-setting for a legal query.

stories.summary: A man asks Rabbi Eliezer how to prioritize honoring his parents, but his tears reveal to the Rabbi that he is actually a grieving orphan.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: your eyelashes, which are filled with tears
verdict_obj.why: The passage describes the physical/emotional state of the questioner having tear-filled eyes, which indicates his personal grief as the son of a widow.

stories.summary: Rav Huna tears expensive silk in front of his son Rabba to test if he will remain respectful and not lose his temper.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: Rav Huna tore silk garments... if he becomes angry
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: רַב הוּנָא קְרַע שִׁירָאֵי... אִי רָתַח
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a physical action (tearing silk) and an intended emotional reaction (anger) as part of a specific historical incident.

stories.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan would stand in honor of elderly Arameans, explaining that their long lives must have involved many trials and experiences.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: Rabbi Yoḥanan himself would stand before Aramean... elders
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֲוָה קָאֵי מִקַּמֵּי סָבֵי דְאַרְמָאֵי
verdict_obj.why: The passage describes the physical act of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rava standing or performing gestures of reverence for elderly gentiles, which goes beyond mere scene-setting for a legal query.

stories.summary: While Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya’akov bar Zavdi were studying, Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed by, and when they stood for him, he informed them they were not required to interrupt their study for his honor.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: passed before them and they stood before him
verdict_obj.why: The passage describes physical movement (passing by) and a physical action (standing up) that occurs in the narrative world, rather than just a legal query or discussion.

stories.summary: A son obeys his father's request to fetch chicks, fulfilling two mitzvot simultaneously, but falls to his death upon his return.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: Rabbi Ya’akov himself saw an incident
verdict_obj.why: The passage explicitly states that Rabbi Ya'akov witnessed a physical event (ma'aseh) occurring in the world, which serves as the empirical basis for the discussion.

stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were reclining in a loft in Lod when they were asked whether study or action is greater, eventually concluding that study is superior as it leads to action.

verdict_obj.why: The passage describes a group of sages sitting together to debate a legal/philosophical question, which constitutes scene-setting for a speech-based discussion rather than a narrative event.

stories.summary: Rav Safra and Rava personally performed menial food preparation tasks for Shabbat to demonstrate that performing a mitzva oneself is more meritorious than using an agent.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: Rav Safra, who would himself singe the head of an animal... and Rava, who would salt a turbot fish
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: רַב סָפְרָא מְחָרֵיךְ רֵישָׁא, רָבָא מָלַח שִׁיבּוּטָא
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates the physical actions of Rav Safra and Rava preparing food for the Sabbath as a precedent for performing a mitzvah personally.

stories.summary: The Sages, seeking a ruling on a dispute between Shmuel and Karna, swap the names of the disputants and send the query to Rav, who responds with an emphatic oath and a ruling.

verdict_obj.why: The 'reversing' of names and 'sending' of the question are rhetorical and administrative components of a legal query, not physical or emotional events.

stories.summary: A man attempts to betroth a minor girl in a marketplace using a bundle of vegetables, leading Ravina to rule the act invalid due to its degrading nature.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: betrothed... with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific physical event that occurred in the world—a man performing a betrothal with a physical object in a public place—rather than a hypothetical case or a purely verbal exchange.

stories.summary: An incident occurs in Rav Hisda's study hall, which he then brings to Rav Huna for a resolution based on a Mishna in Me'ila.

quasi_speech_acts: בֵּי רַב חִסְּדָּא (in the study hall)
verdict_obj.why: The passage describes a legal query being brought from one study hall to another and resolved via a hypothetical case in a Mishnah, with no actual physical or emotional events narrated.

stories.summary: A man steals money and throws it to a woman washing her feet to betroth her, then asks Rava for a ruling on the validity of the act.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: washing her feet... grabbed a few dinars... threw them to her
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: מָשְׁיָא כַּרְעַאּ... חֲטַף זוּזֵי... וּשְׁדָא לַהּ
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific physical sequence of events including washing feet, grabbing money, and throwing it to a woman.

stories.summary: A sharecropper betroths a woman with onions from his employer's field and Rava rules on whether the owner would have minded.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: betrothed a woman with a handful of onions
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific historical incident where a sharecropper performed the physical act of betrothal using a specific object (onions).

stories.summary: A brewer uses beer sediment to betroth a woman; the owner's subsequent comment is analyzed by Rava to determine if the betrothal is valid.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: betrothed a woman with sediment
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a physical act of betrothal using a specific object (beer sediment) that did not belong to the person performing the act.

stories.summary: Mar Yehuda confronts Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at the study hall entrance with a legal contradiction that silences them, leading them to seek a resolution from Rabba.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: They were silent
verdict_obj.why: The verb 'ishtiku' (they were silent) in this context denotes a specific emotional/intellectual state of being stumped or embarrassed by a difficulty, which constitutes an internal event beyond mere speech.

stories.summary: Ravin the Pious was sent to betroth a woman for his son but ended up betrothing her for himself.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: went to betroth a woman to his son, but in the end he betrothed her to himself
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: אֲזַיל לְקַדּוֹשֵׁי לֵיהּ אִיתְּתָא לִבְרֵיהּ, קַידְּשַׁהּ לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific historical incident involving travel and the physical act of betrothal (kiddushin) performed by Ravin the Pious.

stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy land for him, but Rav bought it for himself.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: gave money to Rav... went and purchased it for himself
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: יְהַיב לֵיהּ זוּזֵי... אֲזַל זַבְנַהּ לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a physical transaction where money changed hands and a purchase of land was executed in the world.

stories.summary: Mar Zutra and Rav Adda divide their property and ask Rav Ashi if witnesses are required to validate the division, to which he responds that witnesses are only necessary to prevent lying.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: divided their shared property between them
verdict_obj.why: The passage begins by narrating a completed physical action—the division of property—before the parties approach the sage for a legal ruling on its validity.

stories.summary: A water reservoir in Yavne is measured and found to be lacking the required volume, sparking a debate between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva over the status of those who had already immersed in it.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: they measured it and it was found to be deficient
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific historical incident in Yavne where people physically measured a water reservoir and discovered it was lacking the required volume.

stories.summary: The Gemara cites an incident where Rav visited a specific family to examine their lineage status.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: Rav arrived at the house of the son of a vinegar strainer
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: אִיקְּלַע רַב לְבֵי בַּר שָׁפֵי חַלָּא
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific physical event where Rav traveled to and arrived at a particular household.

stories.summary: An anonymous man identifies his place of origin to the Sages, prompting Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa to stand and clarify the location's geography.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: stood on his feet
verdict_obj.why: The passage describes Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha physically standing up on his feet, which is a physical action beyond mere speech.

stories.summary: As Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is dying, he issues a series of prophetic warnings regarding the flawed lineage of specific Babylonian towns. The Gemara describes a series of synchronized births and deaths of great Sages, ensuring that the world is never without a righteous leader.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying... they went and trapped the fish on Shabbat
verdict_obj.evidence_hebrew: כִּי הֲוָה נִיחָא נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרַבִּי... וַאֲזֻיל וְצָדוּ בְּהוּ בְּשַׁבְּתָא
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates the physical death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the physical actions of people trapping fish on Shabbat, as well as the resulting apostasy.

stories.summary: Ameimar permits Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Meḥoza, leading Rav Ashi to question the legal basis of the decision.

verdict_obj.why: The passage describes a legal ruling (permitting a marriage) and a subsequent debate over the validity of that ruling, all of which constitute speech-acts or intellectual deliberation.

stories.summary: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya ruled according to Rav's opinion in a specific case, which caused Shmuel to become angry.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: Shmuel took offense at this... He was angered
verdict_obj.why: The passage explicitly records Shmuel's emotional reaction (anger/offense) to a legal ruling, which constitutes an internal event beyond mere speech.

stories.summary: A mourning woman removed her husband from his grave and engaged in intercourse with the man guarding the cemetery.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: she removed her husband from his grave
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a series of physical actions including visiting a grave, engaging in intercourse, and disinterring a body, as well as the emotional state of succumbing to temptation.

stories.summary: Ten men used the pretense of carrying a woman on a funeral bier to seclude her for immoral purposes.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: ten men carried out a woman on a bier
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates a specific historical incident where ten men physically carried a woman on a bier to commit an act of immorality.

stories.summary: While walking with Rav Yehuda, Rav spots a woman ahead and insists they speed up to avoid a prohibited state of seclusion.

verdict_obj.evidence_english: were walking along the way
verdict_obj.why: The passage narrates the physical movement of Rav and Rav Yehuda traveling on a road and encountering a woman walking ahead of them.
